video.title: Train, test, trust?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Joseph at the staff-room computer, reading an email with a big ‘98% accurate!’ banner and a picture of a dashboard with pupils’ names blurred. He raises an eyebrow.
scenes.animation: The banner pops in (≤ 200 ms); push-in on Joseph’s face.
scenes.narration: “Ninety-eight per cent accurate!” That’s a company’s email to our school, about its AI for spotting pupils likely to drop out. Ninety-eight per cent of what?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card with the Darsi mark, the course name and the lesson title.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: train a model, test it honestly, and question its score.

scenes.visual: A few training dots on a chart. A very bendy curve wriggles through every one of them. New dots appear and land far from the curve.
scenes.animation: The curve draws itself through each dot (1 s); new dots drop in with cross badges.
scenes.narration: Give a model lots of freedom and few examples, and it can bend to fit every one, mistakes and noise included. It scores perfectly on those training examples. But on new ones, it can be badly wrong.

scenes.visual: A pile of labelled pupil-record cards. A hand slides a few into a locked box marked ‘test’ before training starts; the rest go into the training cog. Later the box opens and the model is scored on those.
scenes.animation: Cards slide into the box; the lock clicks; later it opens and checks and crosses pop.
scenes.narration: So before training, we put some examples aside: a test set the model never sees. The training score shows how well it fitted its own examples. The test score shows how it’s likely to do on new pupils.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip: two bars side by side, a tall training score and a much shorter test score, with the gap between them marked in red.
scenes.animation: Bars grow; the gap bracket draws in red (300 ms).
scenes.narration: This is overfitting: learning the training examples so closely that the model does worse on new ones. The warning sign: a high training score, and a much lower test score.

scenes.visual: Two pupils at desks. One recites last year’s exam answers word for word and gets full marks on that paper; the other works through a method. A new paper arrives: the first freezes, the second writes.
scenes.animation: Split screen; the new paper slides in; a cross and a check pop.
scenes.narration: You’ve seen this in class. One pupil memorises last year’s exam paper and scores full marks on it. Another learns the methods. Give them both new questions, and you soon see who really learned.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside two score cards: 100% on training examples, 70% on the test set. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Character slides in; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A model scores a hundred per cent on its training examples, and seventy on its test set. Which score should you trust?

scenes.visual: The 70% card gets the check badge. The 100% card fades. A row of pupils from the test set appears beside a row of Joseph’s own pupils, with a question mark between them.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the two rows slide in.
scenes.narration: Seventy, from the test set. The hundred only shows how well it fitted its own examples, and the gap warns of overfitting. Even seventy holds only if the test examples look like your pupils.

scenes.visual: The dropout tool’s list of flagged pupils (faces as plain silhouettes). One flagged pupil is happily in class: false alarm. One unflagged pupil’s desk is empty: a miss.
scenes.animation: A flag pops on the first; the empty desk fades in on the second.
scenes.narration: And every score hides two kinds of mistakes. Take the dropout tool. A false positive flags a pupil who was never going to leave. A false negative misses a pupil who does leave. Which costs more? Usually the miss: that pupil got no help. But false flags cost too, if pupils get labelled.

scenes.visual: A hundred pupil icons, two of them leaving. A ‘tool’ that always says ‘nobody leaves’ still shows 98%. Then three question cards: tested on whom, on which data, with which mistakes?
scenes.animation: The icons fill in a 10 × 10 grid; the 98% badge pops; the question cards flip in one by one.
scenes.narration: Now, that ninety-eight per cent. If two pupils in a hundred drop out, a tool that always says “nobody leaves” is also ninety-eight per cent accurate, and useless. So ask three questions. Tested on whom? On which data? With which mistakes?

scenes.visual: A phone screen: circles (training examples), squares (new examples) and a curve. A finger drags the freedom slider up; the curve wriggles through every circle while the ‘error on new examples’ bar grows. Then ‘Many (40)’ is tapped and the curve calms.
scenes.animation: The curve bends as the slider moves; the error bar grows, then shrinks.
scenes.on_screen_text: Lab: too good to be true
scenes.narration: In the lab, circles are training examples and squares are new ones. Give the model more freedom, and watch its curve chase every circle while the error on squares climbs. Then switch to many examples: the curve calms down.

scenes.visual: Joseph holds the tool’s report: one pupil marked ‘no risk’, and beside it a note that she left school in March. Two answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The tool said a pupil was fine, but she left school in March. Which mistake was that?

scenes.visual: The ‘false negative’ card gets the check badge, then the summary lines build.
scenes.narration: A false negative: the tool said no, but the answer was yes. Remember: a perfect training score can hide overfitting. Trust scores on examples the model never saw. And ask: tested on whom, on which data, with which mistakes?

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom: one pupil reads ten answers off a card, another works out the area of a rectangle on the board. Joseph holds up a new question; the class watches who can answer it.
scenes.animation: The answer card flips over; the new question slides in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play “Memoriser and learner”. One pupil memorises the answers to ten area questions; another learns how to work out area. Then ask them both new questions. The class sees overfitting for itself.

checkpoints.prompt: 100% on its training examples, 70% on its test set. Which score should you trust?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the test set holds examples it never trained on. The 100% only shows how well it fitted its own examples.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the training score only shows how well it fitted its own examples. The score on examples it never saw is the one that counts.

checkpoints.prompt: The tool said a pupil was fine, but she left school in March. Which mistake was that?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it said “no risk”, but she did leave: a missed case is a false negative.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a false positive is a false alarm. Here the tool missed a pupil who left: a false negative.
